title: Klausmate
text: 1 Chapter 1: Setting up Klausmate

title: Klausmate
text:
1.1 Summary






NoteThis chapter




Outlines the thinking behind Klausmate
Shows how to install and prepare Klausmate for first use
Introduces the key file and why it is needed
Encourages a critical and reflexive approach towards AI

title: Klausmate
text:
1.2 Who is Klaus?
Think of Klaus as a classroom assistant who helps you write code blocks in RStudio. Their goal is to help you learn, not to replace you learning.






NoteNote



Klausmate is based on the idea that learning to code remains useful in an age of AI—perhaps more so. In any written or spoken language, AI could do the translation for you. However, knowing a little about the language helps you become more proficient and prevents unintended errors. A good tutor does not speak for you but helps you grow in confidence when speaking and writing. This is where Klaus comes in.








ImportantImportant



This is a developmental version of Klausmate, exploring how AI can support teaching with R. It is a ‘proof-of-concept’ not a final package. It is updated regularly and will contain bugs and glitches. What you see on screen may differ from the screenshots in this manual.

title: Klausmate
text:
1.3 Installing Klausmate
To use Klausmate you must have first installed R (the programming language) and—after R has been installed—RStudio){target=“_blank”} (a Development Environment for R). Once those are ready then open RStudio and, in the Console, enter the following:
if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE))
  install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("profrichharris/klausmate")
This will install Klausmate on your computer. It requires an active Internet connection to work.






NoteNote



Installing Klausmate means it is ready for use. But you will need to load it each time you restart R (library(klausmate)—see below).








CautionCaution



The Klausmate installation may fail if other packages are missing from your computer and Klausmate is unable to install them. If this happens, you will need to install those ‘extra’ packages manually.

title: Klausmate
section: 1.4 Running Klausmate for the first time
text:
1.4 Running Klausmate for the first time

Step 1: Load the library
To run Klausmate for the first time, load the library and call to Klaus:
library(klausmate)
klaus()



Figure 1.1. Klausmate opening screen




Step 2: Activate the key file
To talk with Klaus you need a key file. Your (human) instructor will provide this. Please upload the file or enter its web address and enter the PIN.



Figue 1.2. You will need a key file to unlock Klausmate




Step 3: Wait whilst Klausmate is prepared for use
After the key file has been verified, Klausmate will check whether its required packages are available. If not, it will try to install them.






CautionCaution



After the key file has been verified, you may need to wait whilst Klausmate prepares itself for first use. Please be patient. This is a one-time process on your computer.




Step 4: Read the important message
Before you can use Klausmate an important message will appear that you must read carefully and acknowledge. Please pay particular attention to not using Klausmate with personal data and to making sure how you use Klausmate is allowed within the university’s policies on the use of AI tools in academic work, especially in regard to assessment. If you have any doubts, please ask your instructor.
After you have made the acknowledgment, Klausmate is ready for use.



Figure 1.3. Please read the contents of this message carefully

title: Klausmate
section: 1.5 What is the key file for?
text:
1.5 What is the key file for?
Klausmate is free to install but it is not free to use. The cost arises from the use of AI—Klausmate is conversational and works through Claude. Interacting with Claude through prompts incurs a fee. This cost has been ‘prepaid’ for you but to limit the total expenditure (as well as your reliance on Klaus), the amount is capped. Your quota is unlocked by the key file.






NoteNote



The key file sets limits on how much you can use Klausmate, how regularly your quota is topped-up—if at all—and when the key file expires.

title: Klausmate
section: 1.6 How ethical is it to use AI?
text:
1.6 How ethical is it to use AI?
AI raises many socio-economic, political and environmental concerns. Some academic staff (and others) have called for it to be boycotted all or most of the time.
Klausmate is as an experiment. It is an approach we could use for teaching, not an assertion that we should use it for teaching. You are encouraged to read this document and approach AI as you should quantitative methods and data analysis generally—in a reflexive and critical manner.1






ImportantImportant



You must never use AI in a way that contravenes university regulations. Be especially careful not to break rules regarding assessment—when, and how, AI is permitted, if at all. If in doubt, ask.

title: Klausmate
text:
1.7 Please provide feedback
After you have spent some time using Klausmate please provide feedback at Feedback on Klausmate – Fill in form. It will help guide any future development and use in teaching. Thank you.

text: 2.1 Summary

title: 2  Chapter 2: Getting Started
text:
NoteThis chapter




Shows how to generate, fix, run and explain a code block in Klausmate
Illustrates why adding context to a prompt is needed
Stresses that Klausmate is intended to help write and debug short blocks of code that can be passed into RStudio for further development
Provides ways to interface between RStudio and Klausmate

title: 2  Chapter 2: Getting Started
text:
2.2 Using the prompt window

Your first conversation
The first time you use Klausmate, and with each subsequent restart of R, a message appears in the Your Prompt window to remind you of the importance of data protection and to not disclose personal information. Read this and press Clear to get started.






ImportantImportant



Klausmate aims to protect your and other people’s data. It sends Claude your prompts, code and the names of variables but not the data values themselves. It removes printed rows of data from any results it shares. Anthropic, the company that runs Claude, does not use these interactions to train its models and deletes them after up to 30 days. However, these safeguards cannot recognise every kind of personal information and anything you type is sent as written. You should therefore never include personal information in a prompt or use Klausmate with data that could identify individuals.





Figure 2.1. The main window in Klausmate




Entering a prompt
Try entering the following prompt into the Your Prompt window:
Map these data
then press Ask for Code.
It will likely generate a message asking for clarification.
The problem is not the instruction that clearly asks for a map. The problem is not knowing which data to map.



Figure 2.2.The initial prompt was too vague to work with




Adding context to the prompt
Clarification could be obtained by modifying the prompt. However, a different approach is needed here. We will ‘attach’ a data set to the prompt to provide additional context for it.
The data we shall map are linked to the Klausmate package so press Load Package Data, wait a moment of two, then select (tick) and Add the first of the two Birmingham data sets (birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011). Then Close the window.



Figure 2.3. Adding the Birmingham data to provide context for the prompt


You will now see birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011 listed below the prompt window. Double click on the binoculars icon to the left of the filename and its tick box to Look at the data. A description of each of the variables in the data can be found under the Variable description tab.
Click back into the Your prompt window and edit the prompt to say
Map
Next, go back to the variable descriptions and scroll down to find ba_share_2011 under Percentages and shares of the Black African population. Double clicking on that variable name or dragging it to Your prompt will add it to the prompt.
The prompt should now say
Map ba_share_2011
Close the Look at window.



Figure 2.4. Looking at the data

title: 2  Chapter 2: Getting Started
text:
2.3 Generating a code block

Ask for Code
We can now generate the code block needed to map the variable. Ensure that Your prompt still says
Map ba_share_2011
and that AutoRun code is not selected (the box should not be ticked) but Check prompt is—these are the defaults.
Then press Ask for Code.
After a brief pause, code will appear in the Code window.



Figure 2.5 Generated code to map the data








CautionCaution



The code has been generated by AI—specifically by Claude Sonnet 5.5. It is typically reliable for tasks such as this but it is important to know that

the code you obtain may be different from above and from other students; and
the code could contain errors, especially for more complex tasks.





Expanding the code window
Press the expansion icon (the small, diagonally pointing arrows) to the right of where it says Code in the Code tab. This will expand the code window.






Take time to read through the code. Can you understand, in general terms, what it is doing?






akFigure 2.6. The expanded code window

title: 2  Chapter 2: Getting Started
text:
2.4 Explaining the Code
You may not fully understand the code that has been generated. Press Explain for a description of what it does.
Next, try changing the level of explanation and Regenerate the explanation.
Then press Close. Also Close the expanded Code window,






TipTip



You can select a part of the Code block to be explained or ask to Tell me more about any explanation that has been generated.
Explanations are saved in the Explanation tab, next to the Code window (to see it, you will first need to Close the expanded code window if it is open).








CautionCaution



Remember, calls to the AI—both the generation of Code and the request for an Explanation—are not cost free but will eat into your cost allowance.
The amount remaining of your allowance can be viewed to the top right of the Klausmate main window. If no restriction has been imposed then it will record the daily cost instead.





Figure 2.7. Generated text to explain the code

title: 2  Chapter 2: Getting Started
text:
2.5 Running and modifying code

Run the code
Make sure the Code tab is in focus with the generated code shown in it.
To run the code, press the Run button and wait. The word Success! will appear if the code runs to completion. The tab will change to any output—here it is a map.
Click on the thumbnail to enlarge it.
Ignore where it says Save this plot to a file (do not tick it).
Close the plot window.



Figure 2.8. The plot generated as output from the code




Modifying the code
Imagine you want to change the map to a red colour palette but do not know how. Go back to Your prompt and type,
Change the map to a red colour palette
Now Ask for Code. The Changes tab will appear, highlighting the revisions to the code.






What is the key parameter that has been changed and why?



You can now Run the revised code.






NoteNote



Only limited changes are highlighted. If the code has been changed substantially, the Changes tab will not appear.





Figure 2.9. Highlighting small changes in the code




Correcting errors
Go back to the Code window and look for a line that says something like style = "quantile".1 Now, within the Code window, manually change it to
style = "jenns"
Make sure you type it as written here. Do not use a prompt; just change it yourself.
The code block should now be similar to—but not necessarily identical to—the below. If not, you could Clear Code in the code window and copy and paste the following into it.
# Map
ba_share_map <- tm_shape(birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "ba_share_2011",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      n = 5,
      style = "jenns",
      values = "reds"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "ba_share_2011")
  )
ba_share_map
Now press Run.
You will find that the code has Failed to run. That is because we introduced an error (deliberately; typically it would be by accident).
The R output helps explain the problem, but you could leave the R output window in focus and press Explain for further clarification.



Figure 2.10. Explaining why the code failed to run


The correction needed to make to the code should be clear but, if not, Klaus can try and fix it automatically.
Press the Fix button to proceed.
If the amended code now runs successfully, the Changes are likely to be highlighted.
Any output—in this case, a revised map using Jenks ‘natural breaks’ classes—will appear in R output.






CautionCaution



The Fix is AI generated so may not be successful. Either way, it will also eat into your cost allowance.





Figure 2.11. Automatically generated changes to fix the code




Recalling earlier code and output
Click on the Past code tab.
Try pressing the small Code and Output buttons to recall past activity.
When you are ready, make sure the code that generated a Map of ba_share_2011 with are red palette is in the Code window, then Close the Past code.






TipTip



The most recently generated or recalled Code or Output is always moved to the top of the Past code window and highlighted in yellow.




Try it yourself






Add a North arrow to the top left of the map and a scale bar to the bottom right.









TipTip



In much the same way as you can recall earlier code using the Past code tab, previous prompts and their code and outputs can be selected from the Past prompts tab.

title: 2  Chapter 2: Getting Started
text:
2.6 Interfacing with RStudio

Viewing and editing the code block in RStudio
Make sure the Code tab is selected (in focus).
Press Save Code Block to pass the contents of the Code window to RStudio where it can be edited further. It will appear in RStudio with the name shown on screen. For example, ‘Code block saved to Add_north_arrow_and_scale_bar_to_map.R’.


2.6.0.1 Dragging a block code to RStudio
In RStudio, use File –> New File –> R Script to create a blank script file.
Go back to Klausmate and move the host browser so you can also see some of the blank script you just created in RStudio.
Click on the Code tab if it is not already in focus.

Hover your mouse over the word Code and use you mouse to drag the Code tab from Klausmate to the blank script. This will have the effect of cutting and pasting the code block from Klausmate to RStudio.


Grabbing code from RStudio into Klausmate
Reciprocally, you can grab code from RStudio and bring it into Klausmate.
Make sure the script (e.g. Add_north_arrow_and_scale_bar_to_map.R) is the tab which has focus (is selected) in RStudio.
Now go back to Klausmate and Press Clear Code to delete the contents of the Code window.
Next press Grab Code.
If what is in focus within RStudio is a code script then it will be loaded into the Code window.



Figure 2.12. Grabbing a code block from RStudio

title: 2  Chapter 2: Getting Started
section: 2.7 Viewing and saving your code log
text:
2.7 Viewing and saving your code log
Press View Code Log to bring up a log of all the code that has been generated in the current conversation. Press Save to pass the log—date and time stamped—to RStudio.






NoteNote



The Code Log is saved and opened in RStudio by default when you pause or end your session in Klausmate.

title: 2  Chapter 2: Getting Started
text:
2.8 Pausing or ending the session
Klausmate is not designed to replace RStudio. It is intended to help write and debug short blocks of code that can be passed into RStudio for further development. This means most of your programming should continue to be done in the main RStudio environment.

Returning to the Console in RStudio
Go back to RStudio and view its Console window. It will show
> klaus()
Klausmate is running
Presently, the Console is ‘locked’ by Klausmate, which means there is no > prompt showing. Consequently, if you type 1 + 1 in the RStudio Console window it will not return the answer 2.
The simplest way to ‘release’ the Console is to press esc.
To re-activate Klausmate, type klaus() in the RStudio Console and go back to your browser window.






CautionCaution



There is a Quick Console in Klausmate that can be used for quick operations. It is better avoided—Pause Klausmate and use the RStudio Console instead.




Pausing or ending the session from within Klausmate
Using the Pause button within Klausmate also ‘releases’ the Console in RStudio. Its advantage over pressing `esc` is it is more robust, offering to save your Code Log file and open it in RStudio. That gives you a copy of your coding to that point. Pressing esc does not offer this.
To quit Klausmate completely, press End Session.






TipTip



Only Pause Klausmate if you plan to return to your current session. Otherwise, use End Session for a ‘cleaner’ exit that will also default to saving your Code Log.




Restoring previous sessions
Klausmate has some capacity to recover a Recent Session.






WarningWarning



Do not be reliant on recovering a Recent Session. Up to 5 sessions are kept, each for 7 days, then deleted.

title: 2  Chapter 2: Getting Started
text:
2.9 Help
Klausmate has a Help Mode. To enter it, press the ? button towards the bottom of the screen. In Help Mode you can press on any button and find out more about what it does. Press ? again to exit.



Figure 2.12. Klausmate in Help Mode

title: 2  Chapter 2: Getting Started
text: It is possible that it, or something similar, does not appear in the code. If that is the case, go back to Your prompt and Ask for Code with the following instruction: ‘Draw the map using tmap and with quantiles for the map classes’.↩︎

text:
3.2 Start a new conversation
If you are still running Klausmate from the previous chapter, press New conversation. This has the effect of starting Klausmate afresh whilst saving the Code Log from the previous conversation. You can Recall that earlier conversation under the Past conversations tab. Alternatively, run klaus() in the usual way from the RStudio Console.






TipTip



If you cannot see the Past conversations tab it is because you have not yet started as second (or third, …) conversation yet in your current Klausmate session.

title: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models
section: 3.3 Obtaining an answer to a question
text:
3.3 Obtaining an answer to a question
In the Your prompt window type,
Tell me about multilevel modelling
Then press Answer. After a short while, a response will appear in the Answer window.
Click to open the full answer.






Take some time to read the answer before you proceed. It will help prepare you for later parts of the chapter.









CautionCaution



Do not confuse Answer with Ask for Code. It is Answer that you should use here.








TipTip



You can, of course, use any other Large Language Model or web search to ask this sort of question without the cost of eating into your Klausmate quota.





Figure 3.1. Answering a question about multilevel modelling

title: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models
text:
3.4 Load the package data
Use Load Package Data to add both birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011 and birmingham_lsoa_2011_2021 as context for the prompt.
In the Your prompt window type,
Tell me about the variable y_change_asinh
Then press Answer.






As before, take some time to read the answer before you proceed.






Figure 3.2. Saying more about the change variables
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models

title: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models
text:
3.5 Translating answers
Changing Klausmate’s default language translates answers into a different language.
Press Preferences and Change from English to another language of your choosing.
Press Close.
In the Answer tab window there is now the option to Translate into [language]. Press it.
Future Answers (and Explanations) will now use that same language so you may want to go back into Preferences and reset the default to English, which is the drop-down menu under Response language.






CautionCaution



The translation is AI generated so should be treated with caution.








TipTip



The translation in Klausmate is relatively low cost but there are ways to do it for free. The web browser may offer it, for example.





Figure 3.3. Translation into Italian
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models

title: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models
text:
3.6 Prompt refinement
Klausmate will try and help you phrase Your prompt in a way that improves the Code it generates. Such improvements are not guaranteed.
Let’s begin by aiming to plot comparative maps of the two data sets. In the Your prompt widow type the following then Ask for Code.
Using the two Birmingham data sets I’ve added, draw maps of y_change_asinh, one above the other, with a single legend shared by both. Split the values at zero and use Jenks classes on each side, with a colour-blind friendly diverging palette, and add a north arrow and scale bar.
You will likely be told that the prompt is too vague. In a previous chapter, the reason was the lack of context (in that case the problem was draw a map of what?). That is not the problem here but there are still potential gaps in what the prompt asks for.
Accept the suggested changes by pressing Use this version in the Before asking for code window. Then, Ask for Code.






Expand the Code window and take time to look through the output. Can you get a broad sense of what it is doing?



Next, Run the code.



Figure 3.4. Suggesting revisions to the prompt


For me, the maps were not wholly satisfying, so I tried…
Do not stack the maps vertically. Have them alongside each other in a 2 columns by 1 row format. Right justify the legend.
… in Your prompt and pressed Ask for Code. I accepted the suggested rephrasing and then continued to Ask for Code.
Try this yourself. If Changes are highlighted, take a moment to view them, then Run the revised code.
The resulting maps were still not quite what I was looking for so require some further refinement—see Warning below.






WarningWarning



You could spend a lot of time and cost refining the maps by changing the prompts and the code they generate. But it is probably not a good idea because you might also find it frustrating and begin to go around in circles.
The code is only ever as good as the prompt you use and how the LLM interprets it. And that can be difficult to get right.
This points back to the purpose of Klausmate, which is not to replace your learning but to assist it.
Rather than over reliance on AI, your better way forward is to take the skeleton of the code it has generated and flesh it out yourself by manually editing the code. Remember, you can use Save Code Block to save the code and open it in RStudio for further development and testing. It is also in the Code Log.





Figure 3.5. Once you have a broad template for the maps, the code can be refined ‘by hand’
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models

title: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models
text:
3.7 Measuring the spatial pattern






Look at any of the maps that have been generated.

Is there a spatial pattern in where the shares of the Black African population have risen in Birmingham and where they have declined?
Has that pattern changed between 2001–11 and 2011–2022?
Are areas of increase found alongside (cluster with) other areas of growth and/or do areas of decrease cluster with other areas of decline?
Does the strength of any clustering appear to increase or decrease over time?





Measuring spatial autocorrelation at the LSOA level
We will calculate Moran’s I to measure the spatial pattern as the (average) correlation between an LSOA and its neighbours. Type the following into Your prompt and Ask for Code:
Calculate and compare the Moran's values for y_change_asinh in 2001-11 and 2011-21 based on contiguous neighbours at the LSOA scale, using the objects birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011 and birmingham_lsoa_2011_2021. Restrict the analysis to the LSOAs present in both objects so the two values are directly comparable, define contiguity using queen adjacency (shared edge or corner), and report each Moran's I value together with its p-value from a permutation test.
You may find the Klausmate offers you a choice of package to use, in which case accept its recommendation and Use this package.



Figure 3.6. Klausmate offering alternative ways to complete the task








Take some time to read the code and form a broad understanding of it before you proceed.



Nest, press Run.






CautionCaution



In my example, above, the sfdep package needs installing. Please be patient whilst it, or any other package, is installed.


The results appear in the R output window. Can you interpret them? Is the pattern of change getting stronger or weaker over time?






TipTip



Try pressing Explain with the R output window still in focus. Compare your interpretation of the results with what is generated.




Measuring spatial autocorrelation at more aggregate scales
Type the following into Your prompt and Ask for Code
Aggregate the data to make comparable calculations (Moran's I) at the MSOA, ward and constituency levels.






Again, take some time to read the code and form a broad understanding of it before you proceed.

How is the code handling aggregating the neighbourhood-level (LSOA) data values into larger area units (MSOAs, wards and constituencies?).
Is this the only (and best) way of doing it?
What does this warn you about ‘blindly’ using AI to code without also employing your own expertise and learning?




Press Run and view the R output.






How do you interpret the results?

When and at what scale was the pattern of spatial autocorrelation strongest?
Is there any scale at which the pattern has strengthened over time?
Are all the values statistically significant?
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models

title: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models
section: 3.8 Fitting a null random intercepts model
text:
3.8 Fitting a null random intercepts model
Leaving aside the details for now, enter the following into Your prompt:
Fit a null random intercepts model for 2001-11 using the birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011 object, with the outcome variable y_change_asinh, and four geographical levels nested from the smallest to the largest: LSOA, MSOA, Ward and Constituency, using the columns lsoa, msoa, ward and constituency in birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011 for each level. Then calculate the percentage of the total variance at each of the four levels, with the shares summing to 100 per cent and the LSOA level treated as the residual variance.
Before pressing Ask for Code tick the AutoRun Code box. Then press Ask for Code.

If asked, choose to use the lme4 package.






The standard R syntax for a linear regression formula takes the form
lm(Y ~ X)
What is the equivalent syntax for the null random intercepts model?



Scroll down the R output window to the bottom of the results.






Answer the following questions:

At what scale (which geographical level) is the percentage highest?
At what scale (which geographical level) is the percentage lowest?

Now go back to the previous R output—the easiest way to do this is using the back button to the left of the code tab.

In 2001-11, at which scale was the Moran’s I lowest and statistically significant?
In 2001-11, at which scale was the Moran’s I highest and statistically significant?










NoteNote



Variance measures how much the measured value—which here is $y_change_asinh$—varies from place-to-place.
If a higher percentage of the variance is found at the LSOA scale than at the MSOA scale then it suggests that LSOAs are more dissimilar to each other than MSOAs are.
That greater similarity between MSOAs is exhibited by their Moran’s I score, which says MSOAs are more like their neighbours than LSOAs are.








Modify Your prompt by hand to calculate comparable percentages from a null random intercepts model but for the period 2011-21.

How do the results compare?
Are the variations between LSOAs increasing or decreasing?
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models

title: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models
section: 3.9 Gathering the results into a publication quality plot
text:
3.9 Gathering the results into a publication quality plot
Raw R output is useful for personal use but rarely of a sufficient quality if you are intending to present or publish the results. Let’s gather some of our analysis into a higher quality table. Enter the following into Your prompt, Ask for Code and Run.
Gather the percentages from the last two null random intercepts models and present them in a publication-quality table, with the geographical levels as the rows running from the lowest level (LSOAs) to the highest (constituencies). The columns should give the name of each level and then the percentage of variance at that level for the two time periods, taking the variance partitioning coefficients from each null model, rounded to one decimal place, with the 2001–2011 model taken from birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011 and the 2011–2021 model taken from birmingham_lsoa_2011_2021. As a further row at the bottom, please include the total variance for each period, given as the raw sum of the level variances to two decimal places and labelled as such.
The R output can be expanded by clicking on its thumbnail. Copy table allows you to paste the table into programs such as Word.






NoteNote



Although the percentage of the variance (the differences between neighbourhoods) has increased at the LSOA level from 2001-11 to 2011-21, the total variance has decreased. In other words, if you want to find differences in what is measured between places then, increasingly, you need to look at the LSOA scale but, even there, they are harder to find because they are becoming less pronounced.








CautionCaution



Copying the table will try and preserve its formatting but it is possible some might be lost requiring further tidying-up in the receiving software.





Figure 3.7. A reasonable quality table
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models

title: 3  Chapter 3: A Case Study with Multilevel Models
text:
3.10 Multilevel models
The null random intercepts models above are a simple form of multilevel model:

multilevel because they contain multiple grouping levels (in our example, geographical but they do not have to be);
null because they include only the outcome variable (a \(Y\)) without relating it to any explanatory/predictor variables (no \(X\) variables are included);
random intercepts because they allow that the average value of the \(Y\) variable can vary from one group to another (so, from place-to-place in our models)—each group has its own intercept (average).

Calling those intercepts random relates to how they are conceived and treated statistically.
To show, in broad terms, how it works, Clear Code in the Code window, copy and paste the following into it instead, and press Run.
require(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011, 
       aes(msoa21cd, y_change_asinh)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 3,
               color = "red") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011$y_change_asinh),
                               col = "dark blue", linewidth = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_blank())
The R output shows a boxplot, where each box represents a group—each is an MSOA—and the ‘whiskers’ represent variation in the y_change_asinh (the \(Y\) variable) present within that MSOA (the observations are at the LSOA level but those observations are grouped by MSOA).
The solid red line is the overall mean for the data—the overall intercept level.
The red diamond shapes are the mean values for each group—in effect, the group level intercepts.
So, what we have are the overall intercept and the group level intercepts. It is the group level intercepts, when estimated by the multilevel model, that are referred to as the random intercepts.
Looking at the boxplots, what we can see is variation between the groups (they do not all have the same average), as well as within the groups (the observations vary around the average).
An extension to all this is to calculate the random intercepts at each level of the model simultaneously and to do so in a way that works out how much they add to or subtract from the intercepts at the other levels of the model. This means you can estimate a predicted value of y_change_asinh at different levels and for different groups in the model—for specific MSOAs, Wards and Constituencies, as well as getting a sense of at what scale (what level) the geographical patterning of the y_change_asinh is strongest.
Doing that is, unsurprisingly, more complicated than drawing boxplots for each level. One difference between the boxplots and the model is the red diamonds (the averages) that you saw at the MSOA level make no allowance for what is happening at the other levels of the model. They are group averages but they are group averages that do not add to or subtract from what is happening at other levels of grouping. A multilevel model will make that allowance.
Nevertheless, the idea is simple enough—take advantage of the group structures so what is being measured can vary within and between groups at the various levels of the model, thereby gaining an understanding of which groups, and which levels, are the ones of most interest.



Figure 3.8. Understanding within and between group differences is at the heart of multilevel modelling



A random intercepts model with a predictor variable
The null random intercepts models shows there is variation in birmingham_lsoa_2011_2021 at the various levels. A next step is to model what is associated with that variation (what might explain it?).
Deselect the contextual object birmingham_lsoa_2011_2021 [sf] by clicking on the tick box alongside it. That box will be shown with a cross and the name of the object will be struck through.
Enter the following into Your prompt and Ask for Code.
Extend the null random intercepts model for 2001-2011 to now include the predictor variable, pct_ba_2001, with the model fitted on birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011 and the four levels and their grouping variables taken from the existing null random intercepts model for the same period. Calculate the percentage of the variance at each of the four levels before and after the inclusion of the predictor variable, presented as a table of the proportion of total variance at each level, and include the full regression output showing the measured effect of pct_ba_2001 on y_change_asinh, including the coefficient and its standard error.






NoteNote



The model explores whether:

(\(Y\)) A change—over the period from 2001 to 2011—in the share of the total Black African population of Birmingham that lives in each of its neighbourhood LSOAs, is related to (\(X\)) what percentage of the LSOAs’ population was classified as Black African in the 2001 Census. This is a linear regression style relationship.
Whether you need to raise or lower the regression line—the average straight line relationship between \(Y\) and \(X\)—for individual MSOAs, Wards and Constituencies to get a better estimate of the change that happened within them; in other words, whether some consistently have added or decreased change, regardless of the amount of \(X\) in them (so the better prediction of \(Y\) is not simply \(X\) but \(X + \text{'a bit more'}\) or \(X - \text{'a bit more'}\) where the \(\text{'bit more'}\) varies from place to place).









Looking in the Code window, what is the general form of the R syntax that fits this model?





3.10.0.1 Evidence of homophily?
The concept of homophily suggests that people tend to bond and form relationships with people who are similar to themselves. If this applies to where people live and that decision is linked to a person’s ethno-cultural heritage then we might expect neighbourhoods where a higher percentage of their population was Black African in 2001 to attract an increased shared (so a positive change) in the Black African population from 2001 to 2011. Expressed more formally:
\(H_0\): there is no evidence of a relationship between \(Y\) and \(X\) in the model
\(H_1\): as \(X%\) increases, so too does \(Y\)






Look at the results of the model. Is there evidence to support \(H_1\)?





Visualising the model
The model is easier to understand by visualising the lines it is fitting to the data. We will look at these at the Constituency level simply because there are fewer constituencies then there are Wards or MSOAs so fewer lines to show on the plot. The same principle of there being a seperate line for each group applies to other levels too.
Type the following into Your prompt:
I want to draw a scatter plot of the linear relationship between y_change_asinh and pct_ba_2001, using all rows of birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011, with all points in a single neutral colour, and with a straight black line showing the overall relationship taken from the fixed intercept and slope of the random intercepts model of y_change_asinh on pct_ba_2001, which has LSOA Constituency as the random effect and also includes Wards and MSOAs as groups. For each Constituency in birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011, I want a separate grey line parallel to the black line, positioned above or below it according to that Constituency's random intercept from the same model, and each grey line should span the full range of pct_ba_2001. Every LSOA should be drawn, the axes should be labelled with the variable names y_change_asinh and pct_ba_2001, and there should be no title. The plot should be interactive in a way that allows the user to click on the line in the chart and see the constituency name.
Ask for Code and, if required, press Run.
The darkest line in the plot is like a standard regression line. Think of it as the overall relationship between the \(Y\) and \(X\) variables.
The other lines shift that overall relationship upwards or downwards to better fit each constituency. Hovering my mouse over the highest line shows me it is associated with the Birmingham Ladywood constituency. All things being equal, the amount of change is expected to be greater (more positive) here than for any other constituency.






Go online and find out more about Birmingham Ladywood constituency. Does what you learn ‘make sense’ given what the model shows?






Figure 3.9. Showing how the random intercepts shift the overall relationship up or down by constituency




A random intercepts and random slopes model
At the moment, only the intercept (the position of the line) varies between groups at the various levels of the model, which is why the lines for all Constituencies are parallel. We can remove this constraint and allow their slopes to vary too.
Try the following:
Extend the previous plot, using the same data, birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011, and still at the constituency level, but now allowing the slope and intercept of the line to vary by constituency by fitting a random intercepts and slopes model, keeping the same response and predictor as the previous plot, with all constituencies shown on one set of axes and one fitted line per constituency.
Now not only does the baseline value (the intercept) varies by group, so too does the estimated effect of \(X\) on \(Y\) (the slope).






Again, looking in the Code window, what is the general form of the R syntax that fits this model?






Figure 3.10. The model now has random intercepts and slopes




Caterpillar plots
We have visualised the random effects as the constituency levels but, in the model, there were fitted for MSOAs and Wards too.
Try the following:
Draw caterpillar plots for the MSOA, Ward and Constituency levels, using birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011 as the data, and arrange them in a 2 by 2 lattice with the fourth cell left empty. For each group, the random effect is calculated as its random intercept plus the random slope at the mean of the predictor variable. Order the groups within each plot by ascending estimated effect, show all groups, and draw 95% confidence intervals around each estimate.






NoteNote



Caterpillar plots are used to show the differences within groups and whether any observations (whether any MSOAs, Wards or Constituencies) have an uptick or downtick in the expected amount of the \(Y\) variable that is statistically different from zero. Places with a confidence interval that spans zero do not but there are places at the MSOA, Ward and Constituency levels with a group effect, meaning their LSOAs have more or less of the \(Y\) variable than is otherwise expected.








WarningWarning



The confidence intervals are used to determine whether any of the places has a random effect that differs from zero, not from each other. If you wanted to compare any one of the places with another in the same plot to assess if their confidence intervals overlapped, you would need to adjust (shorten) their confidence intervals.





Figure 3.11. Caterpillar plots




Mapping the random effects
The multilevel model we are using is geographical. It is based on neighbourhoods grouped into a geographical hierarchical. That means we can map the results.
Try:
Create a map of the birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011 data showing the MSOA-level effect for each LSOA, calculated as the random intercept plus the random slope at the mean of the predictor variable, using the MSOA identifier column and the LSOA identifier column in birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011 to link each LSOA to its MSOA (default: columns named MSOA and LSOA if present, otherwise the first matching code columns). Each LSOA should be coloured by its MSOA's effect, with the fill and borders in the same colour. The class labels should be rounded to 2 decimal places. Use a diverging colour palette for the fill running from low to high values, with red for negative values, white at zero and blue for positive values, so that positive and negative effects are clearly distinguished (default: a red-white-blue diverging scale with white at zero). Divide the values into 6 map classes in total using equal intervals with zero forced as a break, with the breaks calculated from all values in birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011 (default: breaks calculated from all values in birmingham_lsoa_2001_2011).







Which MSOAs appear to have ‘inflated’ expected values of the \(Y\) variable, and which ‘deflated’ values?
What happens if you redraw the map, this time treating MSOAs with insignificant random effects as white, NA values?
Can you produce a map at the Ward or Constituency scales?

3.11 Prompts matter!
Aside from learning a little about multilevel models and how to fit them in R, an important ‘take away’ from this tutorial should be that prompts matter—phrase them badly and poorer outcomes will arise. The same is true when using Large Language Models more generally.
It is an argument for why learning how to code and having subject expertise to guide the process remains important.






CautionCaution



Earlier in this tutorial we allowed the code to AutoRun after being generated. In practice, this should be discouraged. Remember, the goad of Klausmate is to help you learn code, not to avoid it.
